summary.overview: Amino acids are joined by planar, rigid peptide bonds into chains read from the N- to the C-terminus. This sequence, the primary structure, determines how a protein folds and functions. Biochemists purify proteins by charge, size and affinity, then analyse and sequence them.

sections.heading: The peptide bond
points: A peptide (amide) bond forms by condensation of one amino acid's α-carboxyl with the next one's α-amino group, releasing water.
It has partial double-bond character (resonance), so it is short, rigid and planar, and almost always trans.
There is no rotation about the C–N bond; the backbone can rotate only about N–Cα (φ) and Cα–C (ψ).
Chains are written and numbered from the N-terminal (free α-amino) to the C-terminal (free α-carboxyl) residue.

sections.heading: Primary structure and ionisation
points: Primary structure is the amino acid sequence, encoded by DNA; it dictates the 3D fold and function.
One substitution can change function, e.g. β6 Glu → Val (GAG → GUG) in sickle-cell haemoglobin.
In a peptide, only the terminal α-NH3⁺ and α-COO⁻ plus the ionisable side chains contribute charge; internal α-groups are locked in peptide bonds.
Proteins range from about 100 residues (cytochrome c) to about 27 000 (titin) and may have one or several chains.
Conjugated proteins carry non-protein groups: lipoproteins, glycoproteins (IgG), phosphoproteins (casein), haemoproteins (haemoglobin), flavoproteins and metalloproteins.

sections.heading: Sequencing
points: Today, sequences are usually deduced from the DNA.
Edman degradation labels, cleaves and identifies the N-terminal residue, one cycle at a time.
Mass spectrometry (MALDI, ESI) measures peptide masses precisely and reveals post-translational modifications.
Comparing sequences of the same protein between species reveals evolutionary relationships.

sections.heading: Purification and analysis
points: Proteins are separated by charge, size, ligand affinity, solubility, hydrophobicity and heat stability.
Ion exchange: a cation exchanger (negatively charged beads) binds proteins that are net positive (pH below their pI).
Size exclusion: large proteins are excluded from the bead pores and elute FIRST.
Affinity chromatography exploits specific binding, e.g. xanthine oxidase (rich in Lys and Arg) binds heparin.
SDS-PAGE: SDS unfolds proteins and coats them with negative charge, so they separate by size alone (small proteins move fastest). Isoelectric focusing separates by pI; 2D gels combine both.
Specific activity = activity ÷ total protein. It rises as the protein becomes purer.

keyTerms.definition: Amide bond between the α-carboxyl of one residue and the α-amino of the next.
End of a chain with a free α-amino group; residue 1.
The linear amino acid sequence of a polypeptide.
Protein with a covalently bound non-protein (prosthetic) group.
Stepwise removal and identification of N-terminal residues.
Gel electrophoresis of SDS-denatured proteins, separating them by mass.
Electrophoresis in a pH gradient that separates proteins by pI.
Units of activity per mg of total protein; a measure of purity.

examTips: Size exclusion: BIG proteins come off FIRST. SDS-PAGE: SMALL proteins move FASTEST.
The peptide bond is planar and trans; rotation happens only around φ and ψ.
Count charges in a peptide: N-terminus (+1), C-terminus (−1), plus Lys/Arg (+) and Asp/Glu (−).
Purification: total activity (yield) falls while specific activity (purity) rises.

questions.stem: How is a peptide bond formed?

options.text: By condensation of one residue's α-carboxyl with the next one's α-amino group, releasing water
options.why: This produces an amide link; hydrolysis (adding water) reverses it.

options.text: By oxidation of two cysteine –SH groups, which join the two amino acids through a sulfur bridge
options.why: That forms a disulfide bond.

options.text: By joining the side-chain carboxyl groups of two amino acids, such as aspartate and glutamate
options.why: Peptide bonds link backbone α-groups.

options.text: By adding a molecule of water across two amino acids, which links their α-carbons together
options.why: Adding water is hydrolysis, which breaks peptide bonds.

questions.stem: Why can't a polypeptide backbone rotate freely about the peptide (C–N) bond?

options.text: Resonance gives the C–N bond partial double-bond character, so the peptide group is planar
options.why: Rotation is possible only about the N–Cα (φ) and Cα–C (ψ) bonds.

options.text: The C–N bond is a full triple bond, so the two atoms are locked in a straight line with no rotation
options.why: It is intermediate between a single and a double bond.

options.text: Side chains are covalently bonded to the peptide nitrogen and physically block the bond's rotation
options.why: Side chains attach to Cα (except proline's ring closure).

options.text: Peptide bonds are usually cis, so the two Cα atoms clash with each other if the bond tries to rotate
options.why: Peptide bonds are almost always trans.

questions.stem: In the tripeptide Tyr–Gly–Phe, which residue carries the free α-amino group?

options.text: Tyr
options.why: Peptides are written from the N-terminus (free α-NH3⁺) on the left to the C-terminus on the right.

options.text: Phe
options.why: Phe is the C-terminal residue, with the free α-carboxyl.

options.text: Gly
options.why: The internal residue's α-groups are both in peptide bonds.

options.text: All three residues
options.why: Only the terminal residues keep free α-groups.

questions.stem: What is the approximate net charge of the peptide Lys–Asp–Arg–Gly at pH 7?

options.why: N-terminus +1, Lys +1, Asp −1, Arg +1, C-terminus −1: total +1.
This misses one positive charge; there are three positive groups and two negative.
This forgets the negative C-terminus and the Asp side chain.
Basic groups outnumber acidic ones.

questions.stem: Sickle-cell disease results from a single base change (GAG → GUG) in the β-globin gene. What does this show about primary structure?

options.text: A single amino acid change (Glu → Val) can alter a protein's properties enough to cause disease
options.why: The sequence dictates structure and function; a charged residue replaced by a hydrophobic one creates a sticky surface patch.

options.text: Primary structure has no influence on function, because haemoglobin S still binds oxygen normally
options.why: This example shows the opposite.

options.text: The mutation changes the number of polypeptide chains in haemoglobin, so it can't form a tetramer
options.why: HbS is still α2β2.

options.text: The mutation adds a disulfide bond between β-chains, which links haemoglobin into long fibres
options.why: Val has no –SH group.

questions.stem: Milk casein carries covalently bound phosphate groups. What type of conjugated protein is it?

options.text: A phosphoprotein
options.why: Its phosphate groups (on Ser residues) bind calcium in milk.

options.text: A glycoprotein
options.why: Glycoproteins carry carbohydrate, e.g. immunoglobulin G.

options.text: A haemoprotein
options.why: Haemoproteins carry haem, e.g. haemoglobin.

options.text: A flavoprotein
options.why: Flavoproteins carry FAD or FMN, e.g. succinate dehydrogenase.

questions.stem: How does Edman degradation determine a peptide's sequence?

options.text: It labels the N-terminal residue, cleaves it off and identifies it, then repeats on the shorter peptide
options.why: Successive cycles read the sequence from the N-terminus.

options.text: It hydrolyses the whole peptide at once in strong acid and reads the order of residues from the mixture
options.why: Total hydrolysis gives composition, not order.

options.text: It reads the sequence from the C-terminus, removing one residue at a time with the detergent SDS
options.why: Edman chemistry works from the N-terminus; SDS is a detergent.

options.text: It measures the peptide's absorbance at 280 nm after each cycle, which identifies each residue in turn
options.why: A280 gives concentration, not sequence.

questions.stem: Why is mass spectrometry valuable even when a protein's gene sequence is already known?

options.text: It measures actual peptide masses, revealing modifications such as phosphorylation that DNA can't predict
options.why: Modifications change mass in characteristic ways that MS can detect.

options.text: It is the only reliable way to measure protein concentration, which the gene sequence cannot give you
options.why: Concentration is usually measured by A280 or dye assays.

options.text: It determines the protein's 3D fold directly, showing how the predicted sequence is folded in space
options.why: 3D structure needs methods such as X-ray crystallography or cryo-EM.

options.text: It works only on intact, folded enzymes, so it confirms that the protein is active and correctly folded
options.why: MS typically analyses peptides from digested proteins.

questions.stem: In size-exclusion (gel filtration) chromatography, which proteins elute from the column first?

options.text: The largest proteins, because they can't enter the bead pores and take the shortest path
options.why: Small proteins wander through the pores and are retained longer.

options.text: The smallest proteins, because they slip quickly through the pores inside the beads
options.why: This is the reverse; small proteins are slowed by entering the pores.

options.text: The most positively charged proteins, which are repelled by the beads and pushed out first
options.why: Charge is the basis of ion-exchange chromatography, not size exclusion.

options.text: The proteins with the highest pI, because they bind least tightly to the gel matrix
options.why: pI is irrelevant to size exclusion.

questions.stem: A mixture at pH 6.0 contains protein X (pI 8.5) and protein Y (pI 4.5). It is loaded onto a cation-exchange column (negatively charged beads). What happens?

options.text: X binds, being net positive below its pI; Y flows straight through, being net negative
options.why: Cation exchangers bind positively charged proteins; bound X can then be eluted with salt or a higher pH.

options.text: Y binds, because it is net negative at pH 6.0, and X flows straight through the column
options.why: Y is net negative at pH 6 and is repelled by negative beads.

options.text: Both bind equally, because both proteins carry some positive and some negative groups
options.why: Their opposite net charges at pH 6 separate them.

options.text: Neither binds, because ion-exchange columns separate proteins by their size, not charge
options.why: Ion exchange separates by charge.

questions.stem: Xanthine oxidase binds tightly to a heparin column. Heparin is a highly negatively charged polysaccharide. What is the basis of this binding?

options.text: Positively charged Lys and Arg residues on the enzyme interact with the negative heparin
options.why: This affinity is used to 'fish' the enzyme out of a crude mixture.

options.text: Covalent disulfide bonds form between the enzyme's cysteines and sulfur groups on heparin
options.why: Heparin has no –SH groups; the binding is non-covalent and electrostatic.

options.text: Heparin is a substrate that the enzyme binds and slowly hydrolyses as it passes the column
options.why: Xanthine oxidase acts on purines, not heparin.

options.text: Large proteins become trapped in the pores of the heparin beads, while small ones pass through
options.why: That describes size exclusion.

questions.stem: Why does SDS-PAGE separate proteins by molecular mass alone?

options.text: SDS unfolds the proteins and gives them a uniform negative charge per unit mass, so only size matters
options.why: Native shape and charge no longer matter; small proteins move fastest through the gel.

options.text: SDS separates proteins by their pI, so each protein stops where its net charge becomes zero
options.why: That is isoelectric focusing.

options.text: SDS keeps proteins in their native fold, so their shape and size together set how fast they move
options.why: SDS is a denaturing detergent.

options.text: Large proteins move fastest, because they bind more SDS and so carry more negative charge in total
options.why: The charge-to-mass ratio is constant, so the gel's sieving effect slows larger proteins.

questions.stem: In two-dimensional gel electrophoresis, what are the two separation steps?

options.text: Isoelectric focusing (by pI), then SDS-PAGE (by mass) at right angles
options.why: Combining two independent properties resolves thousands of proteins as separate spots.

options.text: Size exclusion (by size), then affinity chromatography (by binding)
options.why: These are column methods, not gel electrophoresis.

options.text: SDS-PAGE twice in the same direction, first by mass and then by charge
options.why: Repeating the same separation gives no new resolution.

options.text: UV absorbance at 280 nm, then Edman degradation of each separated spot
options.why: These are analysis methods, not 2D separation.

questions.stem: A crude extract has 10 000 units of enzyme activity in 500 mg of protein. After a column step there are 8000 units in 40 mg. How have specific activity and yield changed?

options.text: Specific activity rose from 20 to 200 units/mg (10-fold purification), with an 80% yield
options.why: Specific activity = activity/protein: 10 000/500 = 20 and 8000/40 = 200. Yield = 8000/10 000 = 80%.

options.text: Specific activity fell from 20 to 16 units/mg, because 20% of the activity was lost, so yield is 80%
options.why: Total activity fell slightly, but activity per mg rose sharply.

options.text: Specific activity rose 12.5-fold, from 20 to 250 units/mg, with a 100% yield of enzyme activity
options.why: 12.5 is the fold-reduction in protein (500/40); the yield is 80%, not 100%.

options.text: Nothing changed, because the enzyme units are the same before and after the column step
options.why: Removing contaminating protein raises specific activity.

questions.stem: Why can comparing the sequence of cytochrome c from many species reveal evolutionary relationships?

options.text: Sequence differences accumulate over time, so closely related species have more similar sequences
options.why: Alignments of proteins with the same function trace evolutionary divergence.

options.text: Mammals share an identical cytochrome c, so any differences reveal errors in the sequencing method
options.why: The sequences differ, which is what makes the comparison informative.

options.text: Cytochrome c sequences are determined by diet, so related species that eat similar food share them
options.why: Sequences are encoded genetically.

options.text: Sequences reveal only an organism's body size, which tends to be similar in closely related species
options.why: Sequence similarity reflects ancestry, not body size.

flashcards.back: Short, rigid, planar, trans; partial double-bond character. Rotation only about φ (N–Cα) and ψ (Cα–C).

flashcards.front: Direction in which peptides are written and numbered?
flashcards.back: From the N-terminus (free α-NH3⁺) to the C-terminus (free α-COO⁻).
The amino acid sequence, encoded by DNA. It determines the 3D fold and function.

flashcards.front: Which groups contribute charge in a peptide?
flashcards.back: The N-terminal α-NH3⁺, the C-terminal α-COO⁻ and ionisable side chains. Internal α-groups are in peptide bonds.

Lipoprotein (β1-lipoprotein), glycoprotein (IgG), phosphoprotein (casein), haemoprotein (haemoglobin), flavoprotein (succinate dehydrogenase), metalloprotein (ferritin – Fe; alcohol dehydrogenase – Zn).
Edman: removes the N-terminal residue one cycle at a time. MS (MALDI, ESI): precise masses, detects post-translational modifications.

flashcards.front: Ion exchange, size exclusion and affinity chromatography separate by…?
flashcards.back: Charge; size (large proteins elute first); specific ligand binding.
Net positive proteins, i.e. at a pH below their pI. The beads are negatively charged.
SDS-PAGE: by mass (SDS denatures, uniform negative charge; small proteins fastest). IEF: by pI. 2D gel = IEF then SDS-PAGE.
Activity ÷ total protein (units/mg). It rises as purity increases; total activity (yield) usually falls.
